accuracy.evidence: Terms are defined as in the Poetics (hamartia as error or failing, peripeteia as reversal, anagnorisis as ignorance to knowledge, catharsis as a contested purgation or clarification of pity and fear), Aristotle's rejection of wholly wicked and wholly good heroes is from Poetics 13, Othello's reversal is placed in the Act 3 temptation scene, Lear's recognition in Act 4, and Miller's 1949 essay title is quoted correctly.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the errors examiners flag in A-level tragedy essays: treating any death or unhappy ending as tragic, confusing hamartia with a villain or with bad luck, placing catharsis inside the plot, calling the hamartia moment the recognition (the Lear item), and applying the classical model as a checklist instead of testing it against Miller or Iago's role.

lab_distinct.evidence: A new canvas lab for this topic: a swipe card that tilts as it is dragged left or right, a five-point fortune line whose points are dragged vertically and tested against the tragic shape, flaw tags pinned on hero cards with a bad luck decoy, a term timeline for Othello, and pity and fear meters driven by three hero traits. It passed the 30% shingle gate against all other flag labs.

lab_teaches.evidence: The order moves from the defining question (does the hero's own choice drive the fall?) to the shape of the plot, then the cause inside the hero, then the turning points, then the audience response Aristotle built it all for. The meters show why a flawed, great, self-ruined hero moves us more than a saint or a villain, which turns the theory into a test students can argue with.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each tested by the step that follows: whether death by lightning is tragic (then it is swiped to just sad), where the hero's fortune ends (then the arc test demands it end far below the start), whether hamartia means evil (then the flaws are pinned on admirable heroes), and which hero moves us most (then only good but flawed fills both meters).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions with wrong-answer messages tagged by error: any death is tragic, unhappy ending is enough, hamartia is the villain, catharsis as a plot moment, mixed-up terms, taste instead of audience response, and villains as low status (Claudius is a king). Each says why the choice fails and what to look for instead.

readability.evidence: Student paragraphs use short sentences, gloss each Greek term in plain words on first use and stay within the learner kid FK limit; the adult text, within its limit, names the specifications and the contested readings of catharsis. Canvas cards hold one event or term, wrapped to the card width at a readable serif size on a phone.

no_filler.evidence: Passed the filler phrase scan and the 12% duplication gate. Each student paragraph does one job (sad versus tragic, hamartia, the two turns, catharsis and later writers); the adult text covers specification context, precise definitions, named mistakes and what the lab does; the family tip is three questions to ask after any tragedy.

mobile.evidence: Checked on the iPhone 13 walkthrough and 390 px screenshots of all steps before and after Show me: the hero cards were tightened so the feedback line no longer overlaps King Lear, arc labels alternate rows so they do not collide, the meters and cliff fit side by side, and every drag has a button route.

accessibility.evidence: axe WCAG 2.1 AA was clean in light and dark themes on desktop and phone. The arc can be built entirely with Point, Raise, Lower and Test buttons, flaw and term buttons name the target hero or moment in their aria-labels, and the canvas aria-label reads each event, fortune value and meter percentage aloud.
